vignette:
He is a 61-year-old South Asian man who has spent most of his adult life working in the nonprofit sector, the kind of person who is used to being the steady one in a crisis. Before the accident, his days are structured around service: long meetings about community programs, grant deadlines, phone calls with families who need help navigating housing, food, or immigration paperwork. He likes being useful. His wife often tells him that he carries half the neighborhood in his briefcase. He laughs when she says it, but it is true that he takes pride in being reliable, calm, and hard to shake.

The collision happens on an ordinary weekday afternoon. He is driving back from a partner agency after a meeting, thinking about a budget shortfall and whether he can rearrange staff hours without cutting services. Traffic is heavy but moving. He remembers checking his mirrors, easing through an intersection, and then seeing a truck coming too fast from his left. What stays with him is not the impact itself at first, but the instant before it—the impossible certainty that the truck is not going to stop. He thinks, very clearly, *This is how I die.* Then there is metal folding, glass exploding inward, the violent snap of his body, and the smell of smoke and dust. For a few seconds, maybe longer, he cannot tell whether he is conscious. He hears horns, someone shouting, a woman screaming from somewhere outside the car. He tries to move and feels a bolt of pain and a terror so complete that later he struggles to put it into words. He is trapped long enough to believe the car might catch fire.

In the emergency department he is told he is lucky. He has no catastrophic internal injury, no paralysis, no head bleed. Friends and relatives repeat the same thing for weeks: lucky, blessed, protected. He says those words too, because they are expected and because on one level he believes them. But inside, something has shifted. He goes home sore and exhausted, and at night he is back inside the car. In sleep he hears the blast of the horn and wakes with his heart pounding, fists clenched, already bracing for impact. Sometimes he wakes before the crash, suspended in that split second of knowing, and that is almost worse. His wife reaches for him and he startles hard enough to pull away.

At first he tells himself this will pass. He has seen hardship in his work; he has sat with refugees, widows, men who have lost jobs and homes. Compared with that, he thinks, what right does he have to be undone by one accident? So he returns to work quickly, but the world no longer feels neutral. At intersections he grips the steering wheel until his hands ache. If another car edges forward too aggressively, his chest tightens and his breath turns shallow. He begins taking longer routes to avoid the road where the collision happened. Then he starts inventing reasons not to drive at all. He asks coworkers to handle site visits. He says he is catching up on paperwork, though he has always disliked hiding behind a desk.

The change shows up in smaller ways too. He used to be patient with the people he serves, even when they are frightened or angry. Now loud voices make him flinch. Sudden sounds—construction noise, a dropped file, a bus braking outside—send a shock through him before he can think. In meetings he loses track of conversations because part of him is scanning for danger. He rereads the same email three times. A colleague notices he has become unusually quiet. At home, his wife says he is present in body but not always in the room with her. He sits facing the front window. He checks that the doors are locked more than once before bed.

He is ashamed of how much he avoids. Family members suggest he should be grateful and move on. In his community, endurance is admired; suffering is often carried privately. He does not want to seem weak, dramatic, or self-absorbed. When his adult children call, he minimizes everything. But his wife sees the cost. She sees him decline invitations because he does not want to travel on the highway. She sees him tense when she asks him to pick up groceries. She hears him pacing at 3 a.m. after another broken night of sleep.

What troubles him most is that the accident has altered his sense of himself. He has built a life around helping others feel safe and supported, yet he no longer trusts his own body or the road beneath him. He feels older in a new, frightening way—not simply aware of mortality, but ambushed by it. Some days he can speak about the collision in a matter-of-fact voice; other days, as he describes the truck entering the intersection, his words slow and his eyes fix on a point beyond the room, as if he is again watching death arrive from the left. Even now, months later, when he approaches a busy crossing, he feels that same cold certainty flicker through him, and his body reacts as though the crash is happening all over again.
